BEIJING, China (CNN) — Officials in China’s northwestern Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region said Thursday that a fourth infant had died in the country’s widening scandal over contaminated baby formula. More than 6,200 babies have already become ill after consuming the adulterated milk powder.

Earlier Thursday, provincial police announced that 12 additional suspects had been arrested as part of the investigation. According to the Hebei Public Security Bureau, the new arrests raised the total number of detainees to 18. Officials said 12 of those being held were connected to milk collection and dairy-product manufacturing, while the remaining six were accused of illegally selling the chemical that was mixed into the milk.

Li Changjiang, China’s chief official for quarantine and inspection, said Wednesday that more than 1,300 infants were in hospitals. Reported medical problems included malnutrition, kidney stones and acute kidney failure.

Inspectors have been sent throughout China to examine stockpiles held by dairy producers. Li said that out of the country’s 175 manufacturers of infant milk powder, 66 had halted production.

On Monday, Chinese investigators arrested two brothers who had sold fresh milk later used to make contaminated infant formula. If found guilty, they could face execution, the state-run China Daily reported. The newspaper said the raw milk had been diluted with water and then treated with a chemical to deceive quality-control testing.

Investigators said the brothers admitted watering down the milk and adding tripolycyanamide, commonly known as melamine. According to the report, they said they acted in an effort to make up for financial losses after earlier milk deliveries had been rejected by the factory.

China Daily said the brothers were charged with producing and selling poisonous and dangerous food, an offense that can carry the death penalty.

Medical specialists say consuming melamine can cause kidney stones, ulcers in the urinary tract, and irritation of the eyes and skin. The substance is widely used in products such as coatings and laminates, wood glue, fabric coatings, ceiling tiles and fire-retardant materials.

Thousands of tons of contaminated milk powder have been pulled from the market, including recalls by Mengniu Dairy Group, China’s largest dairy producer, and the Sanlu Group. Li said Wednesday that investigators had detected melamine in almost 70 dairy products made by more than 20 companies. Sanlu products contained the highest levels of the chemical.

China Daily reported that this was not the first time Sanlu had been associated with a contaminated milk-powder scandal. In 2004, at least 13 babies in eastern Anhui province died from malnutrition after consuming milk powder with little or no nutritional value. The paper said that illegally produced formula had been falsely sold under the Sanlu name.

Most of the contaminated formula was consumed inside China, but Li said it was known to have been exported to Taiwan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Yemen, Chad and Burundi.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration said Chinese infant formula has not been permitted for sale in the United States. In a notice posted on its website, the FDA said it had contacted all five formula manufacturers operating in the United States, and none reported using formula or ingredients sourced from China.

The incident is the latest in a series of contaminated-product cases involving goods made in China.

CNN’s Yuli Yang contributed to this report.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about the 2008 Chinese melamine-tainted infant formula scandal, including deaths, hospitalizations, arrests, companies involved, and international export concerns.
counterfactuals.output:
**China’s melamine-tainted milk scandal sickened hundreds of thousands of children and shook global confidence in food exports**

**BEIJING** — A public health scandal involving melamine-tainted infant formula in China left at least six babies dead and nearly 300,000 children ill, triggering criminal prosecutions, international recalls and sweeping questions about food safety oversight in one of the world’s largest export economies.

The crisis erupted publicly in September 2008, when Chinese authorities acknowledged that infant formula produced by the Sanlu Group had been contaminated with melamine, an industrial chemical used in plastics, fertilizers and fire retardants. The substance had been added to watered-down milk to make it appear higher in protein during quality testing.

Infants who consumed the contaminated formula developed kidney stones and other urinary tract problems. Chinese officials later said about 294,000 children had been sickened. More than 50,000 were hospitalized at the height of the crisis, and six deaths were officially reported.

Sanlu, then one of China’s best-known dairy brands and partly owned by New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra, became the center of the scandal. But investigators soon found the problem extended beyond one company. Tests detected melamine in products from several major Chinese dairy producers, including Mengniu Dairy, Yili Industrial Group and Bright Dairy, prompting nationwide recalls and public outrage.

The scandal exposed deep flaws in China’s food safety system, including poor monitoring of milk collection stations, pressure to meet protein standards and alleged delays in reporting contamination. Sanlu had received consumer complaints months before the scandal became public, according to later court proceedings and official accounts.

Chinese authorities arrested dozens of people, including dairy executives, milk suppliers and dealers accused of producing or selling contaminated ingredients. Sanlu chairwoman Tian Wenhua was sentenced to life in prison for her role in the cover-up and distribution of tainted products. Several others received long prison sentences. Two men convicted of producing and selling melamine-laced “protein powder” were executed in 2009.

Sanlu was declared bankrupt, and the Chinese government launched inspections and reforms across the dairy industry. Officials also promised compensation for families whose children were harmed, though some parents and activists later complained that compensation was inadequate and that efforts to seek accountability were restricted.

The scandal quickly became an international concern. Although most of the contaminated infant formula was consumed inside China, Chinese-made milk ingredients and dairy products had been exported to markets around the world. Countries across Asia, Africa, Europe and North America moved to test or ban Chinese dairy imports, and recalls expanded to candies, biscuits, beverages and other processed foods containing Chinese milk powder.

Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan and other governments pulled affected products from shelves or imposed restrictions. The European Union banned imports of Chinese food products containing milk intended for infants and young children and required testing of certain Chinese goods. The World Health Organization and food safety agencies urged countries to monitor products that might contain contaminated milk ingredients.

The scandal became one of China’s most damaging food safety crises, following earlier international concerns over tainted pet food, contaminated medicines and unsafe exports. It also had lasting effects on Chinese consumer behavior, fueling demand for foreign infant formula and prompting years of mistrust toward domestic dairy brands.

For many families, the impact was deeply personal. Parents rushed children to hospitals for kidney scans and treatment, while grieving families demanded answers about how contaminated formula could have reached babies on such a massive scale.

The 2008 melamine scandal remains a landmark case in global food safety — a warning about weak supply-chain oversight, adulterated ingredients and the risks of prioritizing profit over public health.

Chinese authorities are widening their investigation into a nationwide contaminated baby milk powder crisis after officials confirmed that infant formula tainted with the industrial chemical **melamine** has sickened thousands of children and triggered sweeping product recalls.

The scandal has centered on **Sanlu Group**, a major Chinese dairy producer based in **Hebei** province, whose baby formula was found to contain melamine, a chemical used in plastics and fertilizers that can falsely boost protein readings in food tests. Health officials say the contamination has been linked to kidney stones and other urinary problems in infants.

Police in Hebei have announced multiple **arrests** in connection with the case, including individuals suspected of adding melamine to raw milk or participating in the sale of tainted supplies. Investigators are also examining whether company officials and local regulators failed to act promptly after receiving complaints from parents and doctors.

The crisis has spread beyond Hebei, with authorities reporting affected products in several regions, including **Xinjiang**, where dairy operations and suppliers are now under inspection. Food safety teams have been ordered to test milk powder, liquid milk, and other dairy products nationwide.

Chinese regulators have ordered **recalls** of contaminated batches and have directed retailers to pull suspect products from shelves. Several dairy companies have issued public apologies, while hospitals have been told to provide free screening and treatment for infants who may have consumed tainted formula.

The contamination has raised alarm internationally. The U.S. **Food and Drug Administration (FDA)** said it is monitoring the situation closely and noted that infant formula manufactured in China is not legally approved for sale in the United States. FDA officials urged consumers not to purchase or use Chinese-made infant formula from unofficial sources, including products sold online or in specialty markets, and said import checks could be strengthened if necessary.

The Chinese government has promised severe punishment for those responsible and says it is working to restore public confidence in the food supply. But the Sanlu scandal has intensified public anger over food safety enforcement and has become one of the country’s most serious consumer health crises in years.

counterfactuals.output:
**BEIJING (AP) —** China’s tainted milk scandal widened sharply Tuesday as authorities acknowledged that thousands of infants had fallen ill and several had died after drinking baby formula contaminated with the industrial chemical melamine, deepening public anger over food safety failures and raising new questions about regulatory oversight in one of the world’s fastest-growing consumer markets.

Health officials said hospitals across the country were treating babies and young children for kidney stones and other urinary problems linked to contaminated infant formula. The illnesses have been traced to milk powder adulterated with melamine, a nitrogen-rich chemical used in plastics and fertilizers that can make diluted milk appear to contain more protein in routine quality tests.

The scandal, first centered on the Shijiazhuang-based Sanlu Group, one of China’s best-known dairy producers, has expanded to include a growing number of companies after government testing found melamine in multiple brands of infant formula and other dairy products. Authorities have ordered recalls, halted sales of suspect products and dispatched inspection teams to dairy processors and farms.

Several infant deaths have been linked to the contamination, and the number of sickened children has climbed into the thousands, officials said. Many of the victims are babies whose parents relied on powdered formula as a staple food.

Parents crowded pediatric wards in several provinces, clutching medical records and empty formula tins as they waited for ultrasound screenings and urine tests. State media showed long lines outside children’s hospitals, while online forums filled with demands for compensation and punishment of those responsible.

“I never imagined something made for babies could be poisonous,” said one mother interviewed by local television outside a hospital in Gansu province, where some of the earliest cases were reported. “We trusted the brand. Now we don’t know whom to trust.”

Melamine can cause kidney stones and kidney failure, particularly in infants, whose bodies are less able to process toxins. Doctors said early treatment can prevent the most serious complications, but severe cases may require hospitalization or surgery.

The contamination is believed to have occurred after suppliers or middlemen added melamine to raw milk that had been watered down, allowing it to pass protein-content tests. Investigators are examining whether dairy companies ignored warning signs and whether local officials delayed reporting illnesses in an effort to protect major employers and avoid embarrassment.

Sanlu has apologized publicly and recalled its infant formula, but the company has faced intense criticism over reports that complaints about sick babies surfaced months before the recall was announced. Chinese officials have removed or disciplined several local authorities, and police have detained suspects accused of producing or selling melamine-tainted milk.

The central government, seeking to contain the damage, has promised a nationwide overhaul of dairy inspections and tougher penalties for companies that violate safety rules. Premier Wen Jiabao has called for swift action to treat sick children and restore public confidence.

“The incident has exposed grave problems in the production, procurement and supervision of dairy products,” the State Council said in a statement carried by official media. “Those responsible will be severely punished according to law.”

The crisis has revived memories of earlier Chinese food and product safety scandals, including tainted pet food exported to the United States, lead-painted toys and contaminated toothpaste. It has also placed renewed pressure on Beijing to strengthen regulation in industries where rapid expansion has outpaced oversight.

China’s dairy industry grew rapidly over the past decade as rising incomes and government nutrition campaigns encouraged greater consumption of milk products. Formula makers marketed their brands aggressively to young families, particularly in cities where many mothers rely on infant milk powder.

But the supply chain remained fragmented. Many processors buy raw milk from collection stations supplied by small farmers, creating opportunities for tampering and making accountability difficult.

International concern has also grown. Several countries and territories have banned or restricted imports of Chinese dairy products, and food safety agencies in Asia, Europe and elsewhere have stepped up testing of candies, baked goods and other products containing milk powder from China.

The World Health Organization urged Chinese authorities to provide transparent information and ensure contaminated products are removed from the market. The agency said melamine has no approved use in food and poses serious health risks when consumed in significant amounts.

For families whose children have fallen ill, official promises have brought little comfort. Many parents say they want not only medical treatment and compensation, but a full accounting of how contaminated formula reached store shelves.

“This was not an accident like bad weather or a disease,” said a father waiting outside a children’s hospital in Hebei province. “Someone did this, and someone allowed it to happen.”

Authorities have said medical costs for affected children will be covered, and some dairy companies have pledged compensation. But legal experts say parents may face obstacles in pursuing claims, particularly if courts are reluctant to accept large-scale lawsuits in a politically sensitive case.

As inspectors fan out across the country and hospitals continue to report new cases, the scandal has become a major test of China’s ability to police its food supply — and of the government’s willingness to confront the local protectionism and corporate misconduct that critics say allowed the contamination to spread.

For now, many parents are turning away from domestic brands, searching for imported formula where available and affordable. In some stores, foreign-made milk powder has sold out, while cans of Chinese formula remain stacked on shelves.

“We are afraid to buy anything,” said a Beijing grandmother shopping for her infant grandson. “Milk is supposed to make children strong. Now we worry it could kill them.”
